title: Home styles, lifestyles
subtitle: penthouse, home truths, life in the fast lane
summary: Name the different kinds of home people live in, and use the rich set of idioms English builds on the words house, home and life.

lesson.heading: Places people live
lesson.text: A **squat** is an empty building where people start living without the owner's permission. At the other extreme, a **penthouse** is a luxury flat at the top of a building. A **hovel** is a very small, dirty house or flat in a bad, **run-down** condition.

examples.text: They were living in a **squat** in an abandoned office block.
The **penthouse** has a roof terrace and a view over the whole city.
I should hate to live in a **hovel** - dirty and in a bad condition.

lesson.heading: More home styles
rows: furnished / unfurnished
rented accommodation with or without furniture
council or social housing
rented accommodation provided by the state for people on low incomes
a council estate
a large group of such housing
high-rise (flats), a tower block
flats in a tall, modern building with a lot of floors
a granny flat
a set of rooms for an elderly person, connected to a relative's house
lesson.note: Furnished accommodation suits someone who does not own furniture yet; a granny flat gives an elderly relative independence but keeps them close.

lesson.heading: Idioms with house and home (1)
lesson.text: If you **get on like a house on fire** with someone, you get on very well with them. Something everyone knows is **a household name** (or **household word**). Anything **on the house** is free of charge - the owner is paying.

examples.text: Happily, my mother-in-law and I have always **got on like a house on fire**.
The restaurant owner offered us coffees **on the house**.

lesson.heading: Idioms with house and home (2)
lesson.text: **Home truths** are pieces of information that are true but not pleasant or welcome. Something **nothing to write home about** is nothing special. When a fact **hits home**, it becomes fully understood or fully felt. Telling a guest to **make yourself at home** invites them to feel comfortable in your home.

examples.text: It's time he was told some **home truths** about the way he's been behaving!
The town is OK but **nothing to write home about**.
The difficulty of managing without a regular salary is **hitting home** now.
Please just **make yourself at home** while I get dinner ready.

left.label: The exciting life
left.text: **Life in the fast lane** is a way of life full of activity and excitement; if you **have the time of your life**, you have a wonderful time; and someone who **gets a new lease of life** becomes more energetic and active than before.
examples: As a rock star, Joe lived **life in the fast lane**.
Paula's **having the time of her life** in Canada.
When Georgie moved jobs, she seemed to **get a new lease of life**.

right.label: The hard or narrow life
right.text: **A dog's life** is a very unhappy and difficult life, and someone who **leads a sheltered life** has a life protected from unpleasantness. (You can also lead a busy, quiet or normal life.)
examples: Ryan had **a dog's life** in the army.
Kyoko has **led a very sheltered life** and may find it hard to adapt to the big city.

lesson.heading: More idioms with life
lesson.text: If something is **not a matter of life and death**, it is not very serious. If you **take your life in your hands**, you do something very dangerous. And to **breathe new life into** something is to bring new ideas and energy to it.

examples.text: If we miss the last train, it's **not a matter of life and death**.
You're **taking your life in your hands** if you cross the road here - go to the zebra crossing!
When Orla joined the staff, she **breathed new life into** the school.

lesson.text: Get on like a house on fire is always positive - the fire is the warmth of the friendship, not a disaster.

exercises.prompt: Match each kind of accommodation with the person most likely to live there.

pairs.right: someone with nowhere else to live, or making a point about property
people who do not have enough money to buy a house of their own
an elderly relative of the people in the main house
someone with a lot of money and a taste for city views
someone not good at or interested in looking after themselves

exercises.prompt: From the moment we met, we got on like a house ___.
exercises.explanation: To get on like a house on fire is to get on very well with someone.

exercises.prompt: Jenna's so selfish, she deserves to be told a few ___.
exercises.explanation: Home truths are true but unpleasant or unwelcome pieces of information.

exercises.prompt: The new restaurant is OK but nothing really to ___.
exercises.explanation: Something nothing to write home about is nothing special.

exercises.prompt: So what that you didn't get the promotion - it's not a matter of ___.
exercises.explanation: If something is not a matter of life and death, it is not very serious.

exercises.prompt: I'm not sure I'd like to have a celebrity lifestyle, living life in the ___.
exercises.explanation: Life in the fast lane is a way of life full of activity and excitement.

exercises.prompt: As a child, the writer ___ a sheltered life in a small village in the back of beyond.
exercises.explanation: You lead a sheltered life - the past tense is led.

exercises.prompt: We need someone to come and ___ some new life into the project.
exercises.explanation: To breathe new life into something is to bring new ideas and energy to it.

exercises.prompt: We soon managed to ___ ourselves at home in our holiday cottage.
exercises.explanation: To make yourself at home is to make yourself feel comfortable in a place that is not your own.

exercises.prompt: Replace the underlined words: 'We had the most marvellous time on holiday this year.'
options: We had the time of our lives on holiday this year.
We led a sheltered life on holiday this year.
We had a dog's life on holiday this year.
We got a new lease of life on holiday this year.
exercises.explanation: To have the time of your life is to have a wonderful time.

exercises.prompt: Replace the underlined words: 'I imagine that being a servant in the past must have been very hard and tedious.'
options: must have been a dog's life
must have been on the house
must have been a household name
exercises.explanation: A dog's life is a very unhappy and difficult life.

exercises.prompt: Replace the underlined words: 'Because we were such frequent customers, the restaurant gave us a meal free.'
exercises.explanation: Something on the house is free of charge - the owner pays.

exercises.statement: If someone eats you out of house and home, they eat an enormous amount of your food.
exercises.explanation: Correct - it is what people say about visiting teenagers and other big appetites.

exercises.statement: If a performance brings the house down, the audience hated it.
exercises.explanation: Wrong - to bring the house down is to be extremely popular with the audience.
